posts.quote: EVERY CASSEROLE DISH HAD A STRIP OF MASKING TAPE ON THE BOTTOM WITH A NAME, SO IT COULD FIND ITS WAY HOME.
posts.caption: Whenever somebody had a baby or a funeral, a casserole went down the street and the dish came back a week later. Nobody ever had to ask whose it was. Mom put a strip of masking tape on the bottom of every dish she owned and wrote our name on it in ballpoint, pressed hard so it would survive the dishwater. By the end of a hard winter the tape had curled and gone gray at the edges. The dish still found its way home every time, usually with something new in it. A name on the bottom was the whole lending system, and it worked better than any receipt.
posts.first: We had a Pyrex with three different names on its tape, each one crossed out and written over. Mom said that dish had been to more houses than the mailman. My sister has it now, and the tape is still on the bottom.

posts.character: Family life (writing on the backs of photos)
posts.quote: MOM WROTE THE NAMES AND THE DATE ON THE BACK OF EVERY PHOTO, AND NOW THOSE FEW WORDS ARE THE WHOLE STORY.
posts.caption: Flip over any old snapshot in the shoebox and there it was, in blue ballpoint: names, a place, a date, sometimes just "Easter, the year of the flood." Mom did it the same afternoon the pictures came back from the drugstore, sitting at the kitchen table with the pen cap in her teeth. She pressed lightly so the ink wouldn't come through the front. We thought it was a chore. Now the prints have faded and half the faces have no one left to name them, but her handwriting still says who they were. Those few words on the back turned out to be the most valuable part.
posts.first: I found a photo last spring with "Uncle Walt, new truck, July" on the back and nothing else. I would never have known him without it. I sat there a good while with that one.

posts.quote: Every old house had one stair that creaked, and every kid knew exactly which one to skip.
posts.first: The third one from the bottom in our house. You learned to step over it on tiptoe, and you also learned that your parents could hear you breathing anyway.

posts.quote: THE HOME PERMANENT / A KITCHEN CHAIR, A BOX OF CURLERS, AND A SMELL THAT LASTED ALL WEEK
posts.caption: A home permanent started with a kitchen chair, a towel around your shoulders, and a box from the drugstore with a smiling woman on the front. Mom wound your hair onto little pink rods, one at a time, and tugged hard enough to make your eyes water. Then came the lotion, and the smell reached the next county. Everyone in the house breathed through their mouths for two days. By Sunday you had curls as tight as a poodle's, and she promised they'd relax by Wednesday. They did not relax by Wednesday.
posts.first: Mine was the year I turned nine, and I read the instructions out loud the whole time. Mom told me to hush, because she was counting. The curls lasted until Easter, and so did the smell.

posts.quote: THE ATTIC TRUNK SMELLED OF CEDAR AND MOTHBALLS, AND IT HELD A WEDDING DRESS NOBODY WAS ALLOWED TO TRY ON.
posts.caption: The attic stairs pulled down from the hall ceiling on a rope, and you went up only when Mom said so. Up there the light came through one small dusty window and fell across a trunk with brass corners. It smelled of cedar and mothballs and a hundred closed-up summers. Inside, under the blankets, lay her wedding dress wrapped in tissue paper gone yellow. You could look, but you could not touch, and you certainly could not try it on. She was saving it for something, though she never said what.
posts.first: I tried it on once when nobody was home, and the sleeves came down past my fingers. I put it back exactly the way I found it, tissue and all. Mom knew anyway, and she never said a word about it.

posts.quote: DAD'S SHAVING MUG AND BRUSH SAT ON THE SINK, AND THE SMELL OF THE SOAP MEANT SATURDAY NIGHT.
posts.caption: On Saturday evenings Dad shaved with the bathroom door open and the radio going. He stirred the soap in a chipped mug with a brush until it turned into thick white lather, then painted it on his face like he was whitewashing a fence. The whole house smelled of that soap, clean and a little spicy. It meant he was getting ready to take Mom out, or get ready for church in the morning, and either way it was an occasion. We watched from the doorway, forbidden to touch the razor. Years later one whiff of that soap and I'm standing in that doorway again.
posts.first: He kept that mug until the handle broke, and then he kept it anyway. I have the brush now, and the bristles are still soft. It sits on my own sink where I can see it.

posts.quote: MOM RAN OUR MITTENS THROUGH THE COAT SLEEVES ON A STRING, AND NOT ONE WAS EVER LOST.
posts.caption: Every winter morning Mom fed a string through the sleeves of our coats, one end to each mitten, so the whole set hung from our shoulders like a harness. We looked like puppets and we hated it. But you could pull your hands out to catch a snowball, let the mittens dangle, and never lose one in the drift. In a family of five kids that meant nobody standing at the door in tears. The wool froze stiff by recess, and every evening the whole row hung over the stove to thaw. By March the string was gray, and so was the snow. Not one mitten made it to the lost-and-found.
posts.first: My brother figured out he could swing his mittens around like helicopters, and that lasted until one hit the neighbor's window. Mom bought a shorter string after that. I still can't see a pair of mittens without looking for the string.

posts.quote: My grandmother's hallway had rose wallpaper, and I counted every rose while the grown-ups talked.
posts.first: It was a long hall with a table at the end and a clock that ticked loud. I knew every rose by the end of the visit. Eleven across, and I never once got a different number.

posts.character: Family traditions (height marks on the door frame)
posts.quote: THE DOOR FRAME / PENCIL MARKS, A BIRTHDAY DATE, AND EVERY INCH WE EVER GREW
posts.caption: Somewhere in every house, a door frame kept the family's record. Usually it was the pantry or the door to the back hall, and Dad held a ruler flat on your head while Mom made the pencil mark. You stood on your toes when you thought nobody was looking, and you got caught every time. Beside each line she wrote your name and the date in her tidy hand. By the time you were twelve the marks climbed past your brothers' and ran out of door. When the house was sold, nobody could bring themselves to paint that frame.
posts.first: My line stops at fourteen, because I stopped letting anybody measure me. The very top mark is Dad's, put there by my sister as a joke. I'd give a lot to see that door frame again.

posts.quote: I HAD A PEN PAL IN ANOTHER STATE FOR FOUR YEARS, AND WE NEVER ONCE MET.
posts.caption: Her name was Marjorie, she lived in Nebraska, and our teacher matched us up in the fifth grade. Every second Saturday a blue envelope came with her round handwriting on the front and a stamp that was never quite straight. She told me about her cows, her cat, and her brother's broken arm, and I told her about my paper route. We swapped school pictures and a four-leaf clover pressed in wax paper. The letters thinned out the year we both started high school, and then there was one last Christmas card. I never did see Nebraska.
posts.first: I kept every one of those letters in a candy box under my bed. The stamps were all in the top corner, and mine were always crooked too. I still know her address by heart.
